title: Trail Side Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Trail Side wells have a 100-foot median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and typical completed costs of $9,500-$17,500.
h1: Trail Side, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
For a rural property near Trail Side, the local well records point to relatively shallow wells with strong reported yields. Within 5 miles, 2,150 permitted wells are on file, including 1,544 recorded as constructed. A buyer should still treat the records as a planning guide, not a guarantee for one lot. The actual result depends on the site, aquifer, casing and grout design, and the driller’s experience.

Trail Side is on the plains in Morgan County, close to Log Lane Village, Morgan Heights, Fort Morgan, Blue Sky, Saddle Ridge, and Weldona. Reviewing nearby permits before buying can help set expectations for depth, pump sizing, water quality testing, and the cost of getting a usable well into service.

sections.heading: Trail Side wells are usually shallow
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Trail Side is 100 feet. The middle half runs from 68 to 125 feet, so that range is a reasonable starting point when reviewing a drilling bid or a neighboring permit. Forty-nine percent of wells are under 100 feet, while 51% fall between 100 and 300 feet. One percent are between 300 and 600 feet, and none are recorded at 600 feet or deeper.

The deepest well on record is 500 feet. Local ground conditions are described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, while permits most often identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. That combination can produce useful shallow wells, but fractured material remains less predictable than a uniform sand and gravel section. A driller should confirm casing and grout requirements for the specific site.

sections.heading: Reported yield is strong, but ask what was tested
sections.html:
Of the local records, 311 report a pump yield. The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half ranges from 15.0 to 466.5 gallons per minute. Ninety-five percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Five percent fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, with none reported below 5 gallons per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

Those figures are encouraging for a household buyer, but a permit yield is not the same as a guaranteed long-term supply. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, and any production history. An exempt household-use well is generally limited to 35 gallons per minute for pumping, and larger or different uses can require different water-rights review.

sections.heading: Water levels are relatively close to the surface
sections.html:
Only 69 wells report a static water level, so this part of the dataset is smaller than the depth and permit totals. Among those records, the median depth to water is 33 feet, with the middle half from 16 to 51 feet below the surface. That helps explain why many wells in the area can be completed at modest total depths, but it should not be used as a site-specific water-level promise.

The decade comparison deserves attention. The median reported water level was 22 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 35 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper recent median in this dataset, but the number of reporting wells and their locations can change by decade. Check the closest permits and current test information before assuming the water table is steadily dropping.

sections.heading: Trail Side has a long permit history
sections.html:
Permits appear across nearly every decade in the record. The largest listed decade is the 1950s with 285 permits, followed by 267 in the 1970s, 244 in the 2000s, 213 in the 1990s, 143 in the 2010s, 128 in the 1980s, 118 in the 1960s, and 68 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Canfield Drilling Company, also listed as Canfield, Harold E, is the most active driller in these records with 360 entries. Canfield, Leslie George has 211, and Authorized (Pe, Pg) has 181. These names show who appears often in the permit history; they are not a recommendation or a substitute for checking current licensing, references, and availability.

sections.heading: What a new well may cost near Trail Side
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $35 to $55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $3,500 to $5,500. That is only the hole. A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,500 to $17,500.

A written bid should identify the assumed depth, casing and grout, pump equipment, electrical distance, trenching, testing, permits, and restoration. A shallow well can still cost more than expected if access is difficult, the pump setting changes, or the well must go deeper. Compare bids on the same scope rather than comparing only the per-foot drilling rate.

sections.heading: Check water quality, low-yield risk, and building limits
sections.html:
Environmental review matters around Trail Side. Mapping within about 10 miles shows 22 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are no historic mine features mapped in that area. These records do not prove contamination at a particular parcel, but they are a reason to test existing well water and discuss PFAS and other appropriate laboratory work before closing.

Also inspect the septic and building plan, not just the well permit. Confirm the proposed well location, septic setbacks, reserve area, access for a rig, electrical route, and room for tanks or treatment equipment. Permits in the area are used for domestic or household use, stock, irrigation, and monitoring, so the permitted use must match the buyer’s intended use. Over-appropriated basins may require an augmentation plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Trail Side, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Trail Side is 100 feet. The middle half runs from 68 to 125 feet. Forty-nine percent are under 100 feet, while 51% are between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest record is 500 feet, so a buyer should budget for variation rather than assume every lot will be shallow.

faq.q: What is the water yield of wells near Trail Side?
faq.a: Among the 311 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 466.5 gallons per minute, and 95% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These are reported permit figures, not a guarantee for a new well. Request the nearby well report and any pump-test details.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Trail Side?
faq.a: The local model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $3,500 to $5,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,500 to $17,500. Your bid can differ if the site needs more depth, difficult access, added treatment, or longer utility runs.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Trail Side, Colorado?
faq.a: Do not assume a private well is safe without testing. Mapping within about 10 miles shows 22 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not establish a problem at your parcel, but they support testing before purchase and after construction. Review the results with a qualified laboratory or water professional.

faq.q: Should I check a neighboring well before buying land near Trail Side?
faq.a: Yes. Nearby permits can show reported depth, yield, static water level, construction details, and intended use. Trail Side records include 2,150 permitted wells, but only 69 report a static water level and 311 report a pump yield. That makes the closest comparable records especially important. Use them to shape a drilling budget, then confirm conditions with a licensed driller.
